anchorData: TEST CIRCUIT (all lessons use the same one): 3 V supply (two 1.5 V dry cells in series), a 3 V torch bulb, crocodile clips. Materials tested in the gap, in this fixed order: (1) copper wire 10 cm, bulb bright; (2) glass rod/piece, bulb off; (3) dry wood (ordinary ruler/stick), bulb off; (4) plastic strip (stripped cable insulation), bulb off; (5) silicon diode (1N4007), forward-connected: bulb lit; reverse-connected: bulb off. Summary: 1 of 4 ordinary materials conducts (copper); the diode conducts in one direction only. ELECTRICIAN HOUSE WIRING: Nairobi house, copper cable 2.5 mm squared for sockets, PVC plastic insulation, mains 240 V, 50 Hz. ROUGH RESISTIVITY at about 20 C (ohm metre): copper 1.7 x 10^-8; silicon (pure) 2.3 x 10^3; germanium (pure) 0.46; glass about 10^10 to 10^14; PVC about 10^13 or more; dry wood about 10^8 to 10^11. ORDER: copper is lowest, then germanium, then silicon, then wood, then glass and PVC (highest). Silicon is about 10^11 times more resistive than copper (2.3 x 10^3 divided by 1.7 x 10^-8 is about 1.4 x 10^11). ENERGY GAPS at about 300 K: silicon 1.1 eV, germanium 0.67 eV, insulators such as glass above about 5 eV, metals 0 eV (bands overlap). TEMPERATURE: pure silicon conductivity rises with temperature; metals such as copper resistance rises slightly with temperature. DOPING: silicon doped with phosphorus (group 5, 5 valence electrons) gives n-type (extra free electrons); doped with boron (group 3, 3 valence electrons) gives p-type (holes). Typical doping is about 1 atom in 10^7 to 10^8, which raises conductivity by a factor of many thousands. SUPERCONDUCTORS: mercury critical temperature (Tc) 4.2 K (-269 C); niobium-titanium (NbTi) 9.2 K, used in MRI magnets cooled by liquid helium at 4.2 K; YBCO Tc about 92 K (-181 C), above the liquid nitrogen boiling point of 77 K (-196 C). Liquid nitrogen demonstration: YBCO disc cooled to 77 K shows magnet levitation (Meissner effect), resistance zero below Tc. MRI magnet field about 1.5 T to 3 T. KENYA CASES: solar panels (silicon p-n junctions, e.g. Garissa solar plant, 50 MW; Kenyan homes use home solar kits), microchips in phones, M-Pesa and computers (silicon chips with billions of transistors), MRI machines in hospitals such as Kenyatta National Hospital in Nairobi. Note: Garissa solar plant is about 50 MW.
characters: Mr Otieno: electrician in Nairobi who wires the house with copper cable covered in PVC; he holds the insulated wire safely while it carries current. Wanjiku and Kamau: Grade 10 students in Nairobi who test the five materials and keep the Driving Question Board (DQB). Ms Achieng: their Physics teacher who runs the tests and the liquid nitrogen demonstration or video. Class DQB: the shared wall board of questions. Class model: the cumulative drawing of electrons, atoms and energy bands that is revised each lesson. Dr Wekesa: a radiographer at a Nairobi hospital who operates the MRI machine (Lesson 6 to 7). Places: Nairobi, Garissa solar plant, Kenyatta National Hospital. Objects: copper wire, glass, dry wood, plastic strip, 1N4007 silicon diode, 3 V bulb, YBCO disc.
outcome: Copper conducts because its outer electrons are free to move through the metal (bands overlap, no energy gap), while glass, wood and plastic have a large energy gap (above about 5 eV) so almost no electrons can move, which makes plastic a safe cover for wires. Silicon and germanium have a small gap (1.1 eV and 0.67 eV) so they conduct a little, more when warmer, and doping with phosphorus (n-type) or boron (p-type) greatly raises conductivity in a controlled way; joining p and n gives a diode that conducts one way only, the basis of solar panels and microchips. Superconductors below their critical temperature have zero resistance, so NbTi magnets in MRI machines carry large current without energy loss.
conventions: Use: conductor, insulator, semiconductor, superconductor (never mix). Resistivity symbol rho in ohm metre; conductivity is the reverse (1/rho). Energy gap (band gap) Eg in electron volts (eV). Say 'free electrons' for conduction electrons, 'holes' for missing electrons in p-type. Intrinsic = pure; extrinsic = doped. n-type: majority carriers electrons; p-type: majority carriers holes. Say 'forward-biased' (bulb lit) and 'reverse-biased' (bulb off). Temperature in K for superconductors (K = C + 273) and C elsewhere. Critical temperature Tc. Use 'Driving Question Board (DQB)' and 'class model'. Use ohm for resistance, V for volts, A for amperes. Do not claim insulators have zero conduction, say 'almost none'. Do not say semiconductors are half conductors. Doped silicon is still electrically neutral overall. Fixed test order: copper, glass, wood, plastic, diode.
